body_markdown:
Oh, the Cimarron, what a loaded name. Armchair experts have forever yelled and screamed and disdained the nameplate. That initial small Cadillac was meant to compete with yuppie bait cars from the likes of BMW, Volvo, and the ‘baby Benz’ 190E. But by just the second model year, the car was improving. And in typical GM fashion, once the car was really nice, it was unceremoniously axed. But I’m getting ahead of myself.


Jayson Coombes


The Cimarron was sort of forced into existence, not by Cadillac Motor Division, but by antsy Cadillac dealers. As most folks know, luxury European cars were gaining ground in the US throughout the ’70s and into the ’80s.


Jayson Coombes


At the time, GM, and particularly Cadillac, was picky about franchised dealers taking on competitive makes. So the dealers pressured for their own import-like subcompact sporty vehicle, and the Cimarron was the result.


GM


The initial 1982 model, which everyone loved to call “just a Cavalier,” still had a distinct front end when compared to its stablemates. And yes, there were Pontiac, Oldsmobile, and Buick versions too, which seem to be frequently forgotten and/or ignored. But despite all that, the initial[Cimarron](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1988-cadillac-cimarron-tweaking-the-usual-suspects-since-1982/) was … suboptimal.


eBay


For starters, it had a 1.8-liter four-cylinder, and the driving experience was rather buzzy and … shall we say sedate? It was strictly a four-passenger vehicle, as there was a plastic divider/storage compartment in the middle of the rear seat. First-year production numbers totaled 25,968 units, and those debut cars carried an MSRP of $12,181. Many of the smaller Euro “yuppie mobiles” were pretty close to even the first Cimmy speed-wise. Remember, it was the early ’80s.


eBay


But GM learned fast. For 1983 there were several improvements, both mechanical and appearance-wise. A new nose had a more formal grille—much closer in looks to big brother de Ville and Fleetwood—and there was a new circular crest on the hood header panel. The ’83 also got new standard fog lights, as well.


eBay


The odd plastic divider was jettisoned, and the rear seat was at last capable of holding three passengers. Best of all, the ’82 Cimarron’s carbureted 1.8-liter four-pot was thrown off a cliff and replaced with a fuel-injected 2.0-liter inline four. It wasn’t much more powerful, but the new engine had better low-end torque and was much more pleasant–and smooth–to drive.


eBay


All the Cavalier-shouters notwithstanding, Cimarrons were well-equipped cars, even with no options. Standard equipment included air conditioning, tinted glass, a digital clock, reclining leather seats with adjustable lumbar support and adjustable headrests, an AM/FM stereo, power windows, and power steering. The ’83 started at $12,215, and 19,194 were built.


eBay


That base price was substantially more than the lesser GM J-bodies, but right in line with its intended competitors. Just to name a few: Volvo GL, $14,790; BMW 320i, $13,290; Saab 900S, $13,826; and Toyota Cressida, $14,226. The Mercedes ‘baby Benz’ 190E was about the same size and type of vehicle, but at about $24K, it was much pricier than the other cars noted above.


Jayson Coombes


And GM kept improving it. Probably the biggest news came in 1985 when the 2.8-liter V-6 was added as an option. This finally gave the car some oomph, and with the new alloy wheels and side cladding, it finally looked distinctive from its lesser-priced siblings.


Jayson Coombes


While it doesn’t sound impressive in the company of today’s 300-hp minivans, the V-6 Cimarron’s 125 hp and 155 lb-ft of torque were a huge improvement over the 2.0-liter four-cylinder. Curb weight was 2,514 lbs with the four-cylinder and 2,601 lbs with the V-6.


Jayson Coombes


1986 added new wraparound taillights and, midway through the model year, attractive new composite headlights with wraparound amber marker lights. This is the style I really like; gussied up this way, I think the Cimarron is rather attractive and distinctive.


Bryan Gerould


I recently discussed the[Cimarron](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1982-cadillac-cimarron/) with fellow Cadillac fanatic Jayson Coombes, who took the pictures of this gorgeous red ’86 at the CLC Grand National in Albuquerque in 2023. He said, “The 1985/86 is what they should have put out in 1982.” I can’t disagree.


Jayson Coombes


Those 1986 Cimarrons also gained a redesigned center console with a leather-wrapped shift boot and shift knob. The suspension was revised, and a new premium Delco Bose sound system was added to the option list.


Jayson Coombes


The V-6 included multi-port fuel injection and was available with either a four-speed manual or three-speed automatic. The ’86 Cimmy’s MSRP was $13,128 with the four-pot or $13,838 with the V-6, and 24,534 were produced.


Jayson Coombes


What’s more, ’86s had even more standard equipment than earlier Cimarrons. A partial list included lush leather seating, A/C, cruise control, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, tilt wheel, alloy wheels, power 6-way driver’s seat, power windows, power trunk release, an AM/FM stereo with power antenna, power door locks, accent striping, an electric rear window defogger, and a locking fuel door.


Jayson Coombes


[Options included a Morgan cloth and leather interior](https://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Cadillac/1986_Cadillac/1986-Cadillac-Cimarron-Brochure/slides/1986_Cadillac_Cimarron-08-09.html) (a credit option), a digital instrument cluster (which today’s featured car has), the Twilight Sentinel automatic headlight system, an AM/FM stereo with cassette player, rear deck lid luggage rack, and a 6-way powered passenger seat.


Jayson Coombes


I believe the color on our featured Cimarron is Russet, though it could also be Burgundy.[Other available ’86 colors](https://oldcarbrochures.org/United%20States/Cadillac/1986_Cadillac/1986%20De%20Ville%2C%20Fleetwood%20Brougham%20%26%20Cimarron%20Colors/slides/86cadcol04-05-06-07.html) included Chamois, Commodore Blue, Academy Gray, Silver Frost, Bordeaux Red, and Heather.


Jayson Coombes


I especially loved the colors on today’s featured car. I really miss seriously color-keyed interiors. Today, if you can even get something like a red interior at all, it’s likely just red seats and maybe red armrests on the door panels.


Jayson Coombes


Not so the Cimarron. *Everything* is red, from the seats to the headliner, the dash, the console, the carpeting, the steering wheel, steering column, and even the shift handle and handbrake handle. Boy, do I miss that.


Jayson Coombes


At any rate, the Cimarron continued virtually unchanged in its composite-headlight 1986 form through 1988. Come 1989, it was gone from the roster, never to return. Was it a good idea? Yes. Was its initial form somewhat … problematic? Also yes. I think if they gave it better NVH and that V-6 from the get-go, it would have done better.


Jayson Coombes


Would that have guaranteed success? Who knows? I also wonder how it would have done if it had continued through 1994, when the original J-body cars were totally redesigned. Would there have been even further refinements? Would it have perhaps carved itself a nice little niche? We’ll never know, but it’s fun to speculate.


Jayson Coombes


And I wouldn’t mind owning a 1986–88 V-6 Cimarron, if I ever get that four-car garage. I think it’d be fun to head out to the shows and watch people react to it!


Jayson Coombes


The post[1986 Cadillac Cimarron: Improvements Implemented](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1986-cadillac-cimarron-improvements-implemented/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
